title: Assignment problem: permutation enumeration vs the Hungarian method
problem_statement: Given an n x n matrix C of integers, compute the minimum of sum_i C[i][pi(i)] over all permutations pi of {0, ..., n-1}, i.e. the cost of a minimum-cost perfect matching in the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} (rows = workers, columns = jobs). For n = 0 the answer is 0.

input.parameter: n = number of rows (= number of columns).
input.size_measure: n^2 matrix entries (small integers in the harness, so arithmetic is unit cost).

algorithms.name: permutation enumeration
algorithms.idea: Evaluate the cost of every one of the n! assignments and keep the cheapest.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each permutation p of 0..n-1: best = min(best, sum_i C[i][p[i]])
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * n!) (n! permutations, Theta(n) to cost each)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive: every perfect matching of K_{n,n} is a permutation.

algorithms.name: Hungarian method (shortest augmenting paths with potentials)
algorithms.idea: Insert rows one at a time. For each new row, run an array-based Dijkstra over the columns on reduced costs C[i][j] - u[i] - v[j] >= 0 to find a cheapest augmenting path to a free column, augment, and update the potentials so reduced costs stay non-negative and are zero on matched pairs.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^3) worst case (at most n search steps of Theta(n) per inserted row); Theta(n^3) growth measured on the column-dominant family used for timing (this entry gives no proof)
algorithms.correctness: Kuhn 1955 and Munkres 1957 (primal-dual method; Kuhn's original version runs in O(n^4)). The O(n^3) shortest-augmenting-path form with potentials is due to Edmonds & Karp 1972 (and independently Tomizawa 1971). Invariants: (u, v) is dual feasible (all reduced costs >= 0) and every matched pair is tight. So each partial matching is optimal for the rows inserted so far, and after n rows LP duality certifies the perfect matching as optimal.

relationship: Factorial -> cubic: Theta(n * n!) vs O(n^3). The waste in enumeration is ignoring the linear-programming structure: the assignment LP has integral optimal vertices (Birkhoff-von Neumann), so dual potentials certify optimality and guide a polynomial search. For integer costs bounded by N, cost scaling gives O(n^2.5 log(nN)) (Gabow & Tarjan 1989), a further T3 step on dense inputs.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree on n = 0..8 (enumeration capped at n = 8) over three instance kinds: uniform costs in [0, 99], costs in [-3, 3] (many ties and negative entries), and the column-dominant worst-case family. For n <= 12 harness.check compares against an independent exact O(n 2^n) DP over column subsets; for n = 30 and 100 (Hungarian only) it checks the row-minimum and column-minimum lower bounds and the identity-assignment upper bound. V2: enumeration fitted against n * n!; the Hungarian method fitted against n^3 on worst-case instances from generate_scaling (C[i][j] = 1000 j + noise in [0, 999]). On uniformly random matrices its search stops early and the measured growth is visibly below n^3, which is why the worst-case family is used for timing.

caveats: The O(n^3) bound counts arithmetic and comparisons on integers as unit cost. It is a worst-case bound; on typical random matrices the implementation is faster. The maximisation version reduces to this one by negating costs.
notes: Rectangular (n x m) versions and sparse graphs are handled by the same shortest-augmenting-path framework (Jonker & Volgenant 1987).
